enonce_markdown: On a storm hydrograph for a river gauging station, the lag time is the time between:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A storm hydrograph plots river discharge against time. The lag time is read between two peaks: the rainfall peak and the discharge peak.

### Solution

Rain falling on the basin takes time to reach the channel by overland flow, throughflow and groundwater flow, so the discharge peak comes after the rainfall peak. The delay between these two peaks is the lag time. The other options measure the duration of the storm or of the limbs of the hydrograph, not the delay.

**Answer: c.**

choix.texte: the start of the rainfall and the start of the rising limb
the peak of the discharge and the end of the falling limb
the peak of the rainfall and the peak of the discharge
the start and the end of the rainfall

enonce_markdown: Which of the following changes in a river basin would most probably shorten the lag time and increase the peak discharge during a storm?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Anything that reduces infiltration and storage, or speeds the movement of water to the channel, shortens lag time and raises the peak.

### Solution

Impermeable surfaces (concrete, tar) stop infiltration, and drains carry the water straight to the channel, so a large volume reaches the river quickly: short lag time, steep rising limb, high peak. Forest intercepts rain and slows flow, and a reservoir stores and releases water slowly, both lengthening the lag. Draining a swamp does remove a store, but only a swamp-sized part of the basin, and it does not create a fast pathway across the whole basin as urbanisation does; the urbanised basin is the strongest effect.

**Answer: a.**

choix.texte: Building houses, tarred roads and storm drains over a large part of the basin
Planting dense forest on the upper slopes of the basin
Draining a large swamp at the head of the basin so that it can be farmed
Building a reservoir with a controlled outflow on the main river

enonce_markdown: A storm produced its peak rainfall at 10:00 on two basins. Basin P is small, circular, steep and has clay soils; its peak discharge was recorded at 10:45. Basin Q is large, elongated, gently sloping and has sandstone geology; its peak discharge was recorded at 13:00. Rain started at 09:30 on both basins. Which statement correctly gives the lag times and the shape of the hydrographs?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Lag time is measured from the rainfall peak to the discharge peak, not from the start of the rain. A short lag with a high steep peak is a flashy hydrograph.

### Solution

Basin P: 10:45 minus 10:00 = 45 minutes. Basin Q: 13:00 minus 10:00 = 3 hours. The first distractor measures from the start of the rain (09:30), which gives 1 h 15 min and 3 h 30 min. Small, circular, steep, impermeable basins deliver water quickly and give a flashy hydrograph (P). Large, elongated, gentle, permeable basins delay and spread the flow and give a subdued hydrograph (Q). The other two options swap the shapes.

**Answer: d.**

choix.texte: P has a lag time of 1 hour 15 minutes and a flashy hydrograph; Q has a lag time of 3 hours 30 minutes and a subdued hydrograph
P has a lag time of 45 minutes and a subdued hydrograph; Q has a lag time of 3 hours and a flashy hydrograph
P has a lag time of 3 hours and a subdued hydrograph; Q has a lag time of 45 minutes and a flashy hydrograph
P has a lag time of 45 minutes and a flashy hydrograph; Q has a lag time of 3 hours and a subdued hydrograph

enonce_markdown: Explain how the replacement of 40 per cent of the forest in a river basin by housing and tarred roads would change the shape of the storm hydrograph at the gauging station. Refer to the rising limb, the peak discharge, the lag time and the falling limb.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Urbanisation is a long-term (static) change of land cover. It reduces interception, infiltration and storage and speeds the movement of water to the channel, so the hydrograph becomes flashier.

### Solution

- **Lag time**: forest canopy intercepts rain and roots and humus allow infiltration, so water reaches the stream by slow throughflow. Roofs, roads and drains carry rainwater directly to the channel, so the lag time becomes **shorter**.
- **Rising limb**: because more water arrives quickly, the rising limb becomes **steeper**.
- **Peak discharge**: less water infiltrates, so a larger share of the rainfall becomes surface runoff and the peak is **higher**; the risk of flooding downstream increases.
- **Falling limb**: less water is stored in the soil and released slowly as baseflow, so the falling limb is **steeper** and the river returns sooner to low flow (the low flows between storms may also fall because groundwater is recharged less).
- **Conclusion**: the hydrograph changes from a more subdued shape to a flashy shape, with a short lag time, a steep rising limb, a high narrow peak and a quick recession. Drainage channels and sewers make this effect stronger. Good answers add that the change is greatest for small, intense storms and smaller for very heavy storms, when even forest soils become saturated.

enonce_markdown: Two storms with the same total rainfall of 30 mm fall on the same basin. The first storm follows a month of dry weather. The second follows two weeks of heavy rain, which leaves the soil saturated. Which statement best describes the hydrograph of the second storm compared with the first?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Antecedent soil moisture is a dynamic factor. It changes from storm to storm even when the basin itself (the static factors) stays the same.

### Solution

When the soil is saturated its infiltration capacity is almost zero, so most of the 30 mm becomes overland flow and quick throughflow instead of filling soil stores. The water reaches the channel faster and in greater volume: shorter lag time, steeper rising limb, higher peak. After a dry month the soil absorbs a large share of the rain, and the response is slower and smaller. The total rainfall is the same, but the response of the basin is not, which is why dynamic factors matter besides static ones.

**Answer: b.**

choix.texte: The lag time is longer and the peak discharge is lower, because the soil already holds water and releases it slowly
The lag time is shorter and the peak discharge is higher, because saturated soil can absorb little more water and overland flow increases
The lag time and peak discharge are the same, because the rainfall total is the same and the basin has not changed
The lag time is shorter but the peak discharge is lower, because wet soil increases evaporation from the surface

enonce_markdown:
A drainage basin of 25 km² receives an average rainfall of 40 mm in one storm. The volume of storm runoff passing the gauging station is 300 000 m³.

(a) Calculate the runoff coefficient (storm runoff as a percentage of the rainfall) for the storm.

(b) The authorities expect that urban growth will raise the coefficient to 55 per cent for the same storm. Calculate the new volume of storm runoff and explain what this would mean for the shape of the storm hydrograph and for flood risk.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The runoff coefficient is the volume of storm runoff divided by the volume of rainfall, multiplied by 100. Rainfall volume equals depth multiplied by area (convert mm to m and km² to m²).

### Solution

(a) Rainfall volume = 0.040 m × 25 × 10⁶ m² = 1 000 000 m³. Runoff coefficient = 300 000 / 1 000 000 × 100 = **30 per cent** (equivalent to a runoff depth of 12 mm out of 40 mm).

(b) New runoff volume = 0.55 × 1 000 000 = **550 000 m³**, an increase of 250 000 m³ (about 83 per cent more than before, since 550 000 / 300 000 = 1.83).

Meaning for the hydrograph: a larger share of the rain leaves the basin as quickly delivered surface runoff, because impermeable surfaces and drains cut infiltration and storage. The rising limb becomes steeper, the lag time shorter and the peak discharge much higher, while the volume of delayed flow (baseflow) falls. The hydrograph becomes flashier. Flood risk increases for the same storm: channels and drains may be overtopped, and settlements on the floodplain are exposed to sudden floods. Managing this needs measures such as retention ponds, permeable paving, protecting wetlands and keeping floodplains free of building.
